title: Same note, different sound: the secret is in the overtones
body: When a violin and a flute both play the A at 440 Hz, they share a pitch but sound completely different. That quality, called timbre, comes largely from overtones: quieter vibrations at higher frequencies that sound along with the main note. Each instrument’s shape and material strengthens different overtones, and the way a note starts and fades away shapes the sound too.

slides.heading: The harmonic series
slides.text: A string vibrating at 110 Hz also vibrates in halves, thirds and quarters, adding 220, 330 and 440 Hz. Together these blend into what we hear as one note.

slides.prompt: Cut the first fraction of a second off a recorded note. What happens?
slides.answer: Instruments become hard to tell apart
slides.detail: A note’s attack carries much of an instrument’s character, alongside the mix of overtones its shape and material strengthen.

slides.heading: The start matters
slides.text: The first fraction of a second of a note, its attack, carries much of an instrument’s character. Cut it from a recording and instruments can become hard to tell apart.

slides.heading: The clarinet clue
slides.text: A clarinet’s cylindrical tube acts like a pipe closed at one end, so its low notes are dominated by odd harmonics, giving its hollow, woody tone.
